extracted.intended_audience: Prospective Sage contributors (developers, documentation writers, translators, designers, and other non-programmer contributors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for people who want to contribute code, documentation, translations, design, or other help to the SageMath open-source project, including how to get started, coding conventions, review expectations, and technical compatibility notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and report issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is to use Sage and encourage your friends to use Sage. If you find bugs or confusing documentation along the way, please report your problems!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engaging with the software in regular use and reporting bugs or unclear docs is presented as the baseline form of contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary contribution types
rubrics_metrics.description: Two popular ways to contribute to Sage are to write code and to create documentation or tutorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ suggests these as the main entry points and describes further steps for each direction elsewhere on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the official Developer Guide and GitHub guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a look at the official development guide for Sage. At a minimum, the first chapter in that guide is required reading for any Sage developer. Also pay special attention to the GitHub guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is required pre-work before contributing code; the Developer's Guide includes conventions and procedures specific to Sage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join community communication channels
rubrics_metrics.description: You can also join the sage-devel mailing list or hang around on the SageMath Zulip chat channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community channels to ask questions, discuss ideas, and get feedback while learning the community norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn git and obtain the source
rubrics_metrics.description: While you are getting to know the community, grab a copy of the Sage source and familiarize yourself with the git version control system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical familiarity with the repository and VCS is expected before submitting contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work from GitHub issues and discuss before implementing
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to become familiar with the Sage development process is to choose an issue from the Sage repository on GitHub and review the proposed changes contained in that issue. If you want to implement something, it is a good practice to discuss your ideas on the sage-devel mailing list first, so that other developers have a chance to comment on your ideas/proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting existing issues helps orient contributors; pre-implementation discussion prevents duplicated effort and surfaces design concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sage programming language expectations and priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sage’s main programming language is Python. Some parts of Sage may be written in other languages, especially the components that do the heavy number crunching, but most native functionality is done using Python, including 'glue code'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working code is considered more valuable than merely fast code; clean, readable code is important. Correctness comes before optimization (reference to Don Knuth's remark about premature optimization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn Python if needed (recommended resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not know Python, you should start learning that language. A good place to start is the Python Official Tutorial and other documents in the Python standard documentation. Dive Into Python and Building Skills in Python are also recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific resources are recommended depending on prior programming experience; test-driven development topics may be covered in these resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-programmer contribution options
rubrics_metrics.description: As with any free open source software project, there are numerous ways in which you could help out within the Sage community, and programming is only one of many ways to contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: write technical tutorials (keep technical jargon to a minimum), improve website design (graphic designers), translate materials or write tutorials in other natural languages. Contact sage-devel to ask about possible projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available developer tools and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: There are resources and tools for Python and Cython development (examples listed include PEP8, PEP257, pydeps, pycallgraph, PyFlakes, Pylint, Sphinx, XDot, and tutorials/books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides an (incomplete) list of tools and further reading (Cython tutorial, Dive Into Python 3, Fast Numerical Computations with Cython, various HOWTOs) to help contributors write better code and docs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow coding conventions (PEP8, PEP257, Sage conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: You should follow the standard Python conventions as documented at PEP 8 and PEP 257. Also consult the Sage Developer’s Guide, especially the chapter Conventions for Coding in Sage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adherence to these conventions is expected for code submissions and helps with readability and maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your branch easy to review (reviewability checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to make it as easy as possible for anyone to review your branch, follow these tips: Have you clearly described the problem your branch is trying to solve? Have you provided any background information relevant to the problem your patch is trying to solve? Have you clearly described how your branch solves the problem under consideration? Have you clearly described how to test the changes in your branch? Have you listed any issues/PRs that your branch depends on? Is your branch based on a recent (preferably, the latest) Sage beta version? Does your branch follow relevant conventions as documented in the Developer’s Guide?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing clear descriptions, testing instructions, dependency lists, and conforming to conventions increases the likelihood of timely review and merge.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR prioritization and closure policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most people who work on Sage do so in their free time. With hundreds of open PRs of varying degrees of impacts on the whole Sage community, people who work on PRs need to prioritize their time and work on those PRs that interest them. If your branch stands no chance of being merged in the Sage source tree, we will not ignore your branch but simply close the relevant PR with an explanation why we cannot include your changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware maintainers triage and prioritize; a lack of review may reflect limited reviewer time rather than deliberate ignoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to politely remind the community about your branch
rubrics_metrics.description: You are encouraged to take extra care in how you remind the Sage community of a branch/patch you want to get merged into the Sage source tree. Monitor the relevant Sage mailing lists and respond politely to any relevant email threads, with clear explanation on why your patch is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polite, context-aware reminders (tying to events like bug-squash sprints or related workshops) are preferred over repeated attention-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting .sage files to .py: integer handling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When renaming a .sage file to a .py file you must account for differences: Notation for exponentiation: in Python ** means exponentiation and ^ means 'xor'. If you need to return an integer to the user, write return Integer(1) instead of return 1. Also 2/3 no longer means Integer(2)/Integer(3) and returns 0 due to integer division; use Integer(2)//Integer(3) for integer division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete compatibility rules to avoid subtle bugs when moving code from Sage's preparser to pure Python files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting .sage files to .py: importing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: You must import everything you need: each time you use some Sage function, you need to import it at the beginning of the file. Example: from sage.rings.polynomial.polynomial_ring_constructor import PolynomialRing. Use import_statements to get the exact necessary line; you can also inspect PolynomialRing.__module__ to find where it lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAQ shows concrete commands and examples (import_statements, inspecting __module__, file path shown in help output) to help locate correct import paths.
